clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive monogenic obesity syndrome caused by loss-of-function variants in POMC, the precursor of ACTH and the melanocortin peptides.

The classic triad is early-onset severe hyperphagic obesity, secondary adrenal insufficiency from absent ACTH, and pale skin with red hair from lack of alpha-MSH signalling at the melanocortin-1 receptor.
Neonatal presentation can be dramatic — hypoglycaemia, cholestatic jaundice and adrenal crisis from ACTH deficiency before obesity becomes apparent.
Hyperphagia and weight gain result from loss of alpha-MSH agonism at hypothalamic melanocortin-4 receptors that normally suppress appetite.
Red hair may be absent or subtle in individuals of darker constitutive pigmentation, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
Melanocortin-4 receptor agonist therapy (setmelanotide) bypasses the missing endogenous ligand and can produce substantial appetite reduction and weight loss.
Lifelong glucocorticoid replacement is essential, and stress dosing must be intensified during illness to prevent adrenal crisis.
Distinguish biochemically from congenital adrenal disorders — here cortisol is low with inappropriately low ACTH, reflecting a central rather than primary adrenal defect.
reference.pathophysiology: Proopiomelanocortin deficiency is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the POMC gene, whose polypeptide product is post-translationally cleaved by prohormone convertases into several bioactive peptides: adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH), alpha- and beta-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), beta-endorphin and others. Absence of functional POMC-derived peptides produces a characteristic combination of deficits. Lack of ACTH leaves the adrenal cortex unstimulated, causing secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency with glucocorticoid deficiency while the renin-angiotensin-driven mineralocorticoid axis is preserved. Loss of alpha-MSH action at melanocortin-1 receptors in the skin and hair follicles removes the eumelanin signal, producing pale skin and red hair. Most importantly for the metabolic phenotype, alpha-MSH is the key agonist at hypothalamic melanocortin-4 receptors within the leptin-melanocortin satiety pathway; without it, the anorexigenic tone downstream of leptin is lost, driving intense hyperphagia and early-onset severe obesity despite intact leptin and leptin-receptor function. Because the block lies at ligand production, therapy with an exogenous melanocortin-4 receptor agonist can restore satiety signalling. The syndrome exemplifies how a single precursor defect yields a predictable multi-system endocrine, pigmentary and metabolic picture.
additionalDifferentials: Leptin deficiency and leptin-receptor deficiency (severe early-onset obesity without adrenal or pigment features)
Prohormone convertase 1/3 (PCSK1) deficiency with malabsorptive diarrhoea and multiple hormone defects
Melanocortin-4 receptor mutation obesity (receptor-level defect, normal adrenal and pigment)
Prader-Willi syndrome and other syndromic obesity
Congenital secondary adrenal insufficiency from hypopituitarism or TBX19/TPIT mutation
Primary adrenal insufficiency including congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Neonatal cholestatic and hypoglycaemic disorders of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Genetic sequencing of POMC and related melanocortin-pathway genes
Paired morning cortisol and ACTH demonstrating central adrenal insufficiency
ACTH stimulation and, where indicated, dynamic pituitary-adrenal testing
Plasma leptin and leptin-receptor evaluation to exclude leptin-axis defects
Assessment of growth, pubertal status and wider pituitary hormone axes
Blood glucose monitoring for neonatal and stress hypoglycaemia
Liver function and conjugated bilirubin in the cholestatic neonatal presentation
redFlags: Neonatal or childhood adrenal crisis with hypoglycaemia, hypotension and collapse
Intercurrent illness without appropriate stress glucocorticoid escalation
Rapid, relentless weight gain with extreme food-seeking behaviour
Cholestatic jaundice and hypoglycaemia in a newborn suggesting ACTH deficiency
Signs of undertreated cortisol deficiency such as persistent vomiting and lethargy
reference.prognosis: Adrenal insufficiency is life-threatening but manageable with lifelong glucocorticoid replacement and stress dosing, and targeted melanocortin-4 receptor agonist therapy has markedly improved control of the previously intractable hyperphagia and obesity. Long-term outcome depends on avoidance of adrenal crises and sustained weight management with its associated metabolic complications.
pitfalls: Interpreting low cortisol as primary adrenal failure and missing the central (low-ACTH) mechanism
Excluding the diagnosis because red hair is absent in a darker-skinned child
Overlooking the adrenal component and focusing only on obesity, risking fatal crisis
Failing to intensify glucocorticoids during illness, surgery or fasting
Attributing severe early obesity to lifestyle and not pursuing monogenic testing

management: Lifelong glucocorticoid replacement for secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency, with stress dosing during illness
Melanocortin-4 receptor agonist therapy with setmelanotide to bypass the absent alpha-MSH signal and reduce hyperphagia and obesity
Dietetic support and structured weight management alongside pharmacotherapy
Emergency recognition and treatment of adrenal crisis and neonatal hypoglycaemia with parenteral glucocorticoid and glucose, plus a steroid emergency card
Monitoring of growth, puberty and other pituitary hormone axes, and management of neonatal cholestatic jaundice
Endocrinology-led care with genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
